probe.text_sample: Your Page Title Overview Buy Hemingway Magazine Fashion Design Music Culture Travel Podcast Latest: Making records slowly About Authors Membership Contact Sign in The tailor who refuses to hurry The tailor who refuses to hurry In a second floor workshop in Turin, one jacket takes six weeks. Nobody has asked her to go faster in years. Lorenzo Bassi 8 October 2026 , 1 min read Fashion A young tailor in black sitting on a white chair beside a charcoal jacket on a dress form. The workshop is up a stone staircase that smells of steam and wool. There is no sign on the door, only a card with a surname written in pencil. Inside, three people work at one long table. Each jacket passes through every pair of hands at least once, and the owner still cuts every pattern herself, from paper she keeps rolled under the window. Six weeks, not six days A jacket here takes six weeks from the first measurement to the last button. Two fittings are the minimum. Most clients come back for a third because they enjoy the visit. “People think slow means expensive,” she says, pinning a sleeve. “Slow means I only have to make it once.” What the hands remember There are no screens on the table.
